name: Behavioral Interviews
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Answer behavioral questions with clear STAR stories, a ready story bank, honest numbers and good questions of your own.

lesson.intro: Most internship interviews include behavioral questions, and many candidates lose offers on them after doing well on the coding. The good news: these questions are predictable, and a small set of well-prepared stories covers almost all of them. This lesson shows you how to structure a story, which questions to expect, how to build a story bank from what you have already done, and what to ask and avoid.
objectives: Structure answers with STAR and spend most of the time on your own actions
Prepare focused answers to the five most common behavioral questions
Build a story bank of six to eight stories mapped to competencies
Quantify results honestly, with numbers or other concrete evidence
Choose good questions to ask and avoid the most common red flags

sections.title: What behavioral questions are really asking
sections.body:
You solved the coding problem with ten minutes to spare. Then the interviewer says, "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate." You freeze, then talk for four minutes about a group project without ever saying what you did. That answer can sink an otherwise strong interview.

Behavioral questions rest on one idea: how you handled real situations in the past predicts how you will handle them at work better than what you say you would do in theory. So the interviewer wants specific stories, not opinions. Each question probes one or two **competencies**. For interns the usual ones are:

- **Collaboration.** Can you work with people who disagree with you and keep the relationship intact?
- **Ownership.** Do you take responsibility, including for mistakes, and follow through?
- **Learning and coachability.** Can you pick up something new quickly and act on feedback?
- **Handling ambiguity.** What do you do when requirements are unclear or something breaks?
- **Communication.** Can you explain your work and its impact clearly and briefly?
- **Motivation.** Do you actually want this role at this company, and why?

Many companies publish their values, and their behavioral questions map straight onto them. Amazon's Leadership Principles are the best-known example. Read the company's values page before the interview and you can often predict the questions.

Behavioral questions are not confined to one round, either. A recruiter screen is mostly behavioral, and many technical interviewers open with five minutes of "tell me about a project you're proud of."
sections.code:
Question you hear                              What they are checking
"Tell me about a time you disagreed..."        collaboration, respect, judgment
"Tell me about a mistake or failure."          ownership, honesty, learning
"Tell me about learning something quickly."    learning speed, resourcefulness
"Tell me about a time the plan changed."       adaptability, handling ambiguity
"Why do you want to work here?"                motivation, research, fit
sections.tip: Before each interview, read the company's published values and pick one story from your bank for each.
sections.pitfall: Answering in generalities ("I'm a great team player and I always communicate"). Without a specific situation, the interviewer has nothing to write down or score.

check.question: Why do behavioral interviewers ask "Tell me about a time when..." rather than "What would you do if..."?
choices: Real past behavior predicts future behavior better than hypothetical answers, which are easy to polish
Hypothetical questions are not allowed in interviews
It keeps the interview shorter
They want to learn about your personal life
check.explanation: Anyone can describe the ideal response to a hypothetical. A specific past situation, with follow-up questions about what you did and why, is much harder to fake and says more about how you actually work.

sections.title: STAR: a shape for every story
sections.body:
Every good behavioral answer has the same shape, and **STAR** names it:

- **Situation.** The context in one or two sentences: where, when, who. Just enough for the story to make sense.
- **Task.** Your goal or responsibility. What did you need to get done, and why did it matter?
- **Action.** What *you* did, step by step, and why you chose it. This is the heart of the answer and should take at least half your time.
- **Result.** What happened, with a number if you have one, and what you learned or would do differently.

Aim for about 90 seconds to 2 minutes, then stop and let the interviewer ask follow-ups. Use "I" for your own actions. Saying "we" for team work is fine, but if every sentence says "we", the interviewer cannot tell what you did.

Below is the same story told two ways, answering "Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate." The weak version is not dishonest, just vague: no clear task, no specific action by the speaker, a result of "went fine" and a lesson anyone could claim. The strong version spends most of its words on Action, uses "I" for the speaker's choices, ends with a concrete result, and shows judgment: the disagreement was settled with evidence, and nobody lost face.
sections.code:
WEAK
"In my software engineering class we had a group project and there was
a lot of disagreement. One guy wanted to use React and the rest of us
didn't, and it was kind of a mess for a while. We argued a lot, but
eventually we figured it out and the project went fine. I think it
taught us that communication is really important."

STRONG
S  "In a four-person class project, we had three weeks to build a
    course-review web app."
T  "I owned the frontend. A week in, a teammate wanted to rewrite it
    in React, which the other three of us had never used."
A  "Instead of arguing in the group chat, I asked him for a 20-minute
    call to compare options. We wrote down what each choice would cost.
    He showed React would make the review form easier to build; I
    showed the learning time against our deadline. We agreed to keep
    plain JavaScript for this deadline, and he would prototype the
    review form in React on a separate branch."
R  "We shipped on time with all six planned features. His prototype
    was good, so we used React on the next project and he taught the
    rest of us. I learned to turn a disagreement into a written
    comparison early, and I've done that on two projects since."
sections.tip: If you are still describing the class and the team after 30 seconds, jump to "so what I did was..."
sections.pitfall: Spending half the answer on Situation and Task. The interviewer scores your actions and results; the setup only needs to be clear enough to follow.

check.question: In a two-minute STAR answer, which part should take the most time?
choices: Situation
Task
Action
Result
check.explanation: Action is where your judgment, skills and collaboration show, so it deserves at least half the time. Situation and Task only need a sentence or two each, and Result should be short but concrete.

sections.title: The questions you will almost certainly get
sections.body:
Five questions show up in almost every internship process. Prepare each one on purpose.

**"Tell me about yourself."** Not your life story: a 60 to 90 second pitch that ends at this job. Use present, past, future: what you are doing now, one or two experiences that led you here, and what you want next and why this role fits.

**"Tell me about a conflict or disagreement."** They are checking whether you can disagree respectfully and still reach a decision. Pick a disagreement about work (an approach, a priority, a deadline), not a personality clash. Show that you listened, used evidence and kept the relationship. It is fine, even good, if you turned out to be the one who was wrong.

**"Tell me about a failure or mistake."** They are checking ownership and learning. Choose a real failure with real but limited stakes, own your part without blaming anyone, and spend the end on what you changed afterward.

**"Tell me about a time you learned something quickly."** Interns are hired to learn, so this one matters. Say what you had to learn, the deadline, how you learned it (docs, a small experiment, asking a specific person) and what you delivered with it.

**"Why this company?"** They are checking that you did your homework and actually want this job. Name something specific (a product you use, a post on their engineering blog, a technical problem they have written about, a value that matches how you work) and connect it to your experience and to what you want to learn. "You're a big, well-known company" could be said about anyone.
sections.code:
"Tell me about yourself"

WEAK (2+ minutes, chronological, ends nowhere)
"So I grew up in Ohio, and in high school I liked math, and then I went
to State, and first year I took intro CS, and then..."

STRONG (about 75 seconds)
Present  "I'm a third-year CS student at State, and this semester I'm a
          TA for our data structures course."
Past     "I got into backend work building a study-group app for my dorm.
          About 300 students used it, and I learned to design an API and a
          database that held up during exam week. Last summer I worked the
          campus IT help desk, which taught me to debug calmly while
          someone watches."
Future   "Now I want to work on backend systems at a larger scale, which is
          why your platform team's internship stood out to me."
sections.tip: Write your "tell me about yourself" answer out once, then practice it from three bullet points so it sounds natural rather than recited.
sections.pitfall: Choosing a "failure" that is secretly a success, or a conflict where the other person was simply bad. Both read as dodging the question.

check.question: Which failure story will an interviewer find strongest?
choices: "I work too hard and sometimes forget to take breaks."
"My teammate didn't do his part, so our project was late."
"Honestly, I can't think of a real failure."
"I skipped testing to hit a deadline, a bug broke our demo, I owned it with the team, and now I test before every demo."
check.explanation: It is a real mistake with limited stakes, the speaker owns it, and it ends with a specific change in behavior. The first is a disguised strength, the second blames someone else, and the last suggests a lack of self-awareness.

sections.title: Building your story bank
sections.body:
You cannot memorize an answer for every possible question, and you don't need to. Prepare six to eight strong stories instead, and learn to aim each one at several questions. A story about a hard bug in a class project can answer "a challenge you faced", "a time you learned something fast" or "a time you failed", depending on which part you stress.

Where stories come from, especially if you have never had a tech job:

- **Projects.** Personal projects, hackathons, open-source contributions, something you built for a club.
- **Coursework.** Team projects, a tough assignment you turned around, being a TA or tutor.
- **Any job.** Retail, food service, warehouse, tutoring, help desk. Calming an upset customer or training a new hire is a real collaboration and communication story.
- **Activities.** Clubs, sports, volunteering, organizing an event.

Build the bank in four steps. First, list every experience you could talk about for two minutes. Second, pick the six to eight with the clearest actions and results, mixing sources. Third, write each one as short STAR bullet notes (not a script) and tag the competencies it shows, as in the grid below. Fourth, practice each story out loud, ideally recorded, until you can tell it in under two minutes from the bullets alone.

Check the grid for gaps. If no story covers failure, or every story is from the same class, go back to your list.
sections.code:
Story                              Conflict  Failure  Learned fast  Leadership  Challenge
Study-group app (300 users)           .         x          x            .           x
Class project: React debate           x         .          .            x           .
Help desk: outage morning             .         .          x            .           x
TA: redesigned office hours           .         .          .            x           x
Hackathon: demo crashed               .         x          .            .           x
Restaurant: holiday schedule clash    x         .          .            x           .
sections.tip: Keep the bank in one document with STAR bullets for each story. Skim it before every interview, and add new stories as they happen.
sections.pitfall: Writing full scripts and memorizing them word for word. Recited answers sound flat and fall apart at the first follow-up question.

check.question: You have never had a tech internship. Which is the best source for a collaboration story?
choices: A made-up story that sounds like a tech job
Training a new coworker during a rush at your restaurant job
A friend's internship story told as your own
Telling the interviewer you have no relevant experience
check.explanation: Any real job shows collaboration, communication and reliability, and interviewers know students often work outside tech. Invented or borrowed stories collapse under follow-up questions, and "no experience" gives them nothing to score.

sections.title: Quantifying results
sections.body:
Compare two endings to the same story: "and the app got faster" versus "and the page load dropped from about 4 seconds to under 1." The second is more believable, more memorable and easier for the interviewer to write in their notes. Numbers turn a claim into evidence.

Things you can usually count:

- **Time:** hours saved per week, minutes off a build, days ahead of a deadline.
- **Scale:** users, requests, rows, files, people on the team, students helped.
- **Quality:** bugs fixed, tests added, error rate, crash reports, grade.
- **Speed:** latency, load time, query time, before and after.
- **Adoption:** how many people used it, and whether anyone kept using it after you moved on.

No numbers? Use before-and-after, scale or adoption. "The professor used my grading script for the next two semesters" is strong evidence without a single percentage.

Be honest about precision. If you estimated, say so: "roughly 30 percent faster, measured by timing the nightly job for a week before and after." Interviewers often ask how you measured something, and a confident made-up number collapses under one follow-up question.
sections.code:
Vague                              Quantified
"I made our tests faster."         "I cut the test suite from 12 minutes to 3 by
                                    running tests in parallel and mocking the
                                    network calls."
"I helped a lot of students."      "I tutored about 40 intro Python students a
                                    semester and ran a weekly review session that
                                    grew from 5 to 25 regulars."
"My script saved time."            "My script replaced a 2-hour weekly manual
                                    report, and the team still runs it."
sections.tip: After every project or shift, write down one number you could measure. Recording numbers as you go is far easier than reconstructing them a year later.
sections.pitfall: Inventing precise numbers. "Improved performance by 37.4 percent" invites "how did you measure that?", and a vague reply undoes the whole story.

check.question: You rebuilt a club's website and have no analytics. Which result is strongest and still honest?
choices: "It improved engagement by about 50 percent."
"The club now posts all its events there, and two other clubs asked me to build theirs."
"It was much better than the old one."
"Everyone loved it."
check.explanation: Adoption is real evidence: the club relies on it and other people asked for one. The 50 percent figure has no measurement behind it, and "much better" or "everyone loved it" are opinions the interviewer cannot weigh.

sections.title: Your questions, and the red flags to avoid
sections.body:
Near the end, the interviewer asks, "What questions do you have for me?" Answering "None, I think you covered everything" wastes your best chance to show curiosity and to learn whether you want the job. Prepare three to five questions, and fit them to the person: an engineer can tell you about code review, a manager about how interns are supported, a recruiter about the timeline.

Good questions are about the work and how people succeed:

- "What does a successful intern accomplish in the first month?"
- "What did the last intern on your team work on, and did it ship?"
- "How does code review work on your team?"
- "What's something you've learned here in the last year?"
- "What are the next steps, and when should I expect to hear back?" (best for the recruiter)

Skip questions the website already answers ("What does your company do?"), and save pay and perks for the recruiter rather than the engineer.

Red flags that can sink an otherwise good interview:

- **Blaming others,** or badmouthing a former teammate, manager or employer.
- **All "we", no "I".** The interviewer cannot tell what you did.
- **No result,** or a story that just stops.
- **Fake weaknesses** ("I care too much") and fake failures that are secretly successes.
- **Exaggerating** your role, or listing skills you cannot discuss when asked a follow-up.
- **Sharing confidential details** from a previous employer.
- **Rambling** past three minutes, or a script that sounds memorized.
- **Having no questions** at the end.
sections.tip: Write your questions down and bring them. Glancing at notes for your own questions is normal and shows you prepared.
sections.pitfall: Saying "no questions" because the interview felt long. One thoughtful question about the team's work leaves a much better final impression.

check.question: Which question is weakest to ask an engineer at the end of an interview?
choices: "How does code review work on your team?"
"What did the last intern on your team work on?"
"What does a successful first month look like for an intern?"
"So what does your company actually do?"
check.explanation: The company's website answers that one, so asking it signals you did no research. The other three are about the real work and how interns succeed, which shows genuine interest and gets you useful information.

keyTerms.definition: Questions about how you handled real past situations, used to predict how you will work.
A skill or trait a question probes, such as collaboration, ownership or learning speed.
Situation, Task, Action, Result: a structure for telling a work story clearly and briefly.
Six to eight prepared stories, each tagged with the competencies it can demonstrate.
An outcome stated with a number or concrete evidence, such as time saved, users or adoption.
A structure for "tell me about yourself": what you do now, what led here, what you want next.
Taking responsibility for outcomes, including mistakes, and following through.
A probe after your story, such as "what would you do differently?", that tests depth and honesty.
An answer pattern that signals risk to the interviewer, such as blaming others or vague "we" answers.

summary: Behavioral questions use your past behavior to predict your future behavior, so answer with specific stories, not opinions.
Use STAR, spend most of the time on your Action, say "I" for what you did, and finish with a result and a lesson.
Prepare the core five on purpose: tell me about yourself, conflict, failure, learning fast and why this company.
Build a bank of six to eight stories from projects, classes and any job, tag them by competency, and practice from bullet notes.
Quantify results honestly; without numbers, use before-and-after, scale or adoption.
Bring three to five questions about the work, and avoid blame, vague "we" answers, fake weaknesses and exaggeration.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend preparing for their first internship interview how to answer "Tell me about a time you failed" using STAR, and what would make their answer weak or strong.

questions.question: Put the parts of a STAR answer in order.
items: Situation: the context in a sentence or two
Action: what you did and why
Result: what happened and what you learned
questions.explanation: Situation and Task set the scene briefly, Action carries most of the answer, and Result closes with evidence and a lesson.

questions.question: In STAR, what does the T stand for?
questions.explanation: Task is your goal or responsibility in the situation: what you needed to get done and why it mattered.

questions.question: Your practice answer runs two minutes, and the first 70 seconds describe the class, the team and the assignment. What is the best fix?
choices: Keep it, because context helps the interviewer
Cut the setup to a sentence or two and spend the time on what you did
Speak faster so everything fits
Drop the Result to save time
questions.explanation: Situation and Task only need to make the story followable. The interviewer scores your actions and results, so time spent on setup is time taken away from what counts.

questions.question: Which change would improve this answer the most?
questions.code:
Answer A
"We had a group project and my team had some disagreements about the
database. We talked it through and decided on PostgreSQL, and the
project went well."
choices: Make it even shorter
Add more about the class and the professor
Say specifically what you did, why, and what concrete result followed
Replace "we" with your teammates' names
questions.explanation: The answer has a situation and nothing else: no task, no action by the speaker and a result of "went well." Adding your own actions, your reasoning and a concrete outcome turns it into a story the interviewer can score.

questions.question: Which make the Result of a STAR answer stronger? Choose all that apply.
choices: A number, such as time saved or people who used it
What you learned or would do differently
Evidence that someone kept using your work
A longer description of the team's background
Saying the project "went well"
questions.explanation: Numbers, adoption and reflection are all evidence. Background belongs in a short Situation, and "went well" is an opinion the interviewer cannot check.

questions.question: Match each question to what it mainly tests.

pairs.right: Disagreeing respectfully and reaching a decision

pairs.left: Tell me about learning something quickly
pairs.right: How you ramp up on unfamiliar things
A short pitch that connects you to the role

questions.explanation: Knowing what each question tests tells you which part of your story to stress: the lesson for a failure, the respectful process for a conflict, the learning method for learning fast, the specifics for why this company.

questions.question: Put the parts of a strong "tell me about yourself" answer in order.
items: Present: what you study or work on now
Past: one or two experiences that led you here
Future: what you want to learn or build next
Fit: why this role matches that
questions.explanation: Present, past, future keeps the answer to about a minute and makes it end at the job you are interviewing for, instead of trailing off in your life history.

questions.question: The interviewer asks for a real weakness. Which answer works best?
choices: "I'm a perfectionist."
"I don't really have weaknesses."
"I used to stay quiet in code reviews when I disagreed. Now I write my concern as a question in the review, and last month that caught a real bug."
"Honestly, I'm bad at most things except coding."
questions.explanation: A real, fixable weakness plus what you did about it shows self-awareness and growth. "Perfectionist" is a disguised strength that reads as evasive, claiming none signals low self-awareness, and the last answer undersells you.

questions.question: You finish a failure story and the interviewer asks, "What would you do differently now?" You hadn't thought about it. What is the best response?
choices: Say you wouldn't change anything, since it worked out in the end
Explain that the deadline was the real problem
Repeat the result of the story more clearly
Take a moment, then name one concrete change to how you work and why
questions.explanation: This follow-up tests whether you actually learned from the failure. A brief pause and one specific change is a strong answer. Blaming circumstances or saying nothing would change suggests the lesson never landed.

questions.question: Midway through your story the interviewer asks, "What was your part, specifically?" What does that usually mean?
choices: You have said "we" so much they cannot tell what you did, so describe your own actions
They think the story is made up
They want you to start a different story
They want to hear more about the team
questions.explanation: Interviewers can only score you, not your team. When every sentence is "we", they have to ask. Answer with "I" statements: what you decided, built or changed.

questions.question: Which way of preparing for behavioral questions works best?
choices: Prepare six to eight stories as STAR bullet notes, tag each with the competencies it shows, and practice them out loud
Memorize a full script for every question you can find online
Prepare nothing so your answers sound natural
Prepare one great story and use it for every question
questions.explanation: A small bank of flexible stories covers most questions, and bullet notes keep you natural under follow-ups. Scripts sound recited, improvising leads to rambling, and one story stretched over every question gets repetitive fast.

questions.question: A student with no tech job is building a story bank. Which are good sources? Choose all that apply.
choices: A team project in a class
A part-time retail or restaurant job
A hackathon, even one they didn't win
A friend's internship, told as their own
A story invented to fit a common question
questions.explanation: Real experiences from classes, any job and events all show collaboration, ownership and learning. Borrowed or invented stories fall apart under follow-up questions, and getting caught ends the interview.

questions.question: Which is the strongest way to state the result "I made the website faster"?
choices: "I made the website way, way faster."
"I improved website performance by 83.27 percent."
"I cut the home page load from about 4 seconds to under 1 by compressing images and caching API responses."
"I made the website faster using industry best practices."
questions.explanation: It gives a believable before and after plus the actions behind it, so it survives the follow-up "how?". The 83.27 percent figure is suspiciously precise with no method attached, and the other two are claims with no evidence.

questions.question: You said your script saved "around 5 hours a week." The interviewer asks how you know. What is the best answer?
choices: "It's just a feeling I had."
"I timed the manual process for two weeks before and after. It's an estimate, but the gap was consistent."
"Everyone on the team agreed it was about that."
"I'd rather not get into the details."
questions.explanation: Explaining a simple measurement method, and being upfront that it is an estimate, makes the number credible. A feeling or group agreement is not a measurement, and refusing to explain makes the whole claim look invented.

questions.question: Which are good questions to ask an engineer who just interviewed you? Choose all that apply.
choices: What does a successful intern accomplish in the first month?
How does code review work on your team?
What did the last intern work on, and did it ship?
What does your company do?
How many vacation days would I get?
questions.explanation: Questions about the work, the team's practices and what success looks like show curiosity and give you real information. The company's website answers the fourth, and benefits are a recruiter conversation.

questions.question: Which are red flags in a behavioral answer? Choose all that apply.
choices: Blaming a teammate for the project failing
Describing a former employer's confidential roadmap
Saying "we" throughout with no "I"
Admitting a mistake and explaining what you changed
Answering in about two minutes, then pausing for questions
questions.explanation: Blame, leaking confidential information and hiding your own role all signal risk. Owning a mistake and keeping answers to about two minutes are exactly what interviewers want.

questions.question: Why do behavioral interviews ask about specific past situations?
questions.answer: Because how you actually behaved in real situations predicts how you will behave at work better than hypothetical answers, which are easy to polish. Specific stories are also hard to fake under follow-up questions.
questions.explanation: That is why vague answers score poorly: without a specific situation, there is no behavior to evaluate.

questions.question: Which answer to "Why this company?" is strongest?
choices: "I applied to a lot of places and you replied first."
"You're a big, famous company, and it would look great on my resume."
"I need an internship this summer, and this one pays well."
"I read your engineering blog post on moving payments to an event queue, and I built a small queue-based project last semester. I'd like to learn how that works at your scale."
questions.explanation: It is specific to this company, shows research, connects to the candidate's own experience and says what they want to learn. The others could be said about any employer, or are about the candidate's needs only.

questions.question: About how long should a typical STAR answer run before you stop for follow-up questions?
choices: About 20 seconds
About 1.5 to 2 minutes
About 5 minutes
As long as it takes to cover every detail
questions.explanation: Around 90 seconds to 2 minutes is long enough for a clear Action and Result, and short enough that the interviewer can steer with follow-ups. Twenty seconds rarely includes real actions, and five minutes loses the listener.

questions.question: You have a 20-minute recruiter call next week. What should you mostly prepare for?
choices: A hard dynamic programming problem in a shared editor
Your background, why you are interested, a project you're proud of, and your graduation date and availability
A system design whiteboard exercise
Detailed questions about the company's stock price
questions.explanation: Recruiter screens are mostly behavioral and logistical: a short pitch about yourself, your motivation, a project story and practical details. Technical depth usually comes in later rounds.

questions.question: In your best conflict story, your teammate's idea turned out to be better than yours. Should you use it?
choices: No, always pick a story where you were right
Only if you leave out the part where you were wrong
Yes, if you show how you disagreed respectfully, compared the options and changed your mind on the evidence
No, conflict stories should be about personality clashes
questions.explanation: Interviewers want to see how you disagree and decide, not whether you win. Changing your mind because of evidence shows exactly the judgment and openness that teams need.

questions.question: You're asked, "Tell me about a time you led a team," but you have never had a formal lead role. What should you do?
choices: Say you have never led anything
Claim you were the lead of a group project when you weren't
Talk about a leader you admire instead
Describe a time you took initiative informally, such as organizing a study group or splitting up a project's tasks, and say it was informal
questions.explanation: Leadership questions are about initiative and influence, not titles. Informal leadership is a real answer, and being clear that it was informal keeps it honest. Inflating your role invites follow-ups you can't answer.

questions.question: What should a strong "time you learned something quickly" story include?
questions.answer: What you had to learn and why, the deadline or stakes, how you learned it (docs, a small experiment, asking a specific person), and what you delivered with it, ideally with a concrete result.
questions.explanation: The learning method is the most important part: it tells the interviewer how you will ramp up on their codebase and tools.

questions.question: Put the steps for building a story bank in order.
items: List every experience you could talk about for two minutes
Pick the six to eight with the clearest actions and results
Write each one as STAR bullet notes and tag its competencies
Practice each one out loud until you can tell it in under two minutes
questions.explanation: Start wide, then choose, then structure, then rehearse. Tagging competencies before practicing shows you which questions each story can answer and where the gaps are.

questions.question: Your story: you inherited a broken class project two weeks before the deadline, learned Flask over a weekend and shipped on time. Which question does this story fit worst?
choices: Tell me about a time you learned something quickly
Tell me about a challenge you overcame
Tell me about working under a tight deadline
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a manager
questions.explanation: The story has learning, a challenge and a deadline, so it can be aimed at the first three by stressing different parts. It contains no disagreement with anyone, so forcing it into a conflict question would dodge the question.

questions.question: You're asked about the biggest project from your last internship, which is not public yet. Which response is best?
choices: Share the internal codename, unreleased features and revenue numbers to show how important it was
Describe the kind of problem, your role and the outcome in general terms, and say you'll keep internal details private
Refuse to talk about the internship at all
Describe a different, made-up project so you reveal nothing
questions.explanation: You can tell a complete STAR story without confidential details, and saying you are keeping them private shows good judgment. Leaking details makes the interviewer wonder what you would leak about them; refusing or inventing loses the story entirely.

questions.question: In STAR, which part (one word) covers the steps you personally took?
questions.explanation: Action is what you did and why. It is the part interviewers score most, so it should take at least half of the answer.

questions.question: A company publishes a list of its values. How should you use it before a behavioral interview?
choices: Ignore it, since values pages are just marketing
Memorize the list and recite it when asked why you want to join
Map a story from your bank to each value, because the questions often follow them
Mention every value by name in each answer
questions.explanation: Many companies build behavioral questions around their published values (Amazon's Leadership Principles are the classic case). Having a story ready for each one means fewer surprises. Reciting or name-dropping values without stories adds nothing.
